title: Hold up his arms (Exodus 17:8–13)
hook: Moses' arms tire on the hill, and Aaron and Hur hold them up

segments.voice: Yesterday, manna, named for a question: bread that came each morning and rotted if you hoarded it. Your line was enough for today.

Try this, if you can. Raise both arms over your head and hold them there. Ten seconds is easy. Thirty, your shoulders start to burn. A minute, and they shake. Now imagine holding them up until sunset. At a place called Rephidim, a people called Amalek attack Israel. A later book says they struck at the stragglers, the tired and weak at the back. Moses sends a man named Joshua to choose fighters and lead them, and climbs a hill with the staff of God in his hand, and two companions: his brother Aaron, and a man named Hur.
screen: `ARMS UP: TEN SECONDS, A MINUTE.` → `AMALEK ATTACKS.` → `UP THE HILL, STAFF IN HAND.`

segments.voice: Then a strange battle report, in the King James translation: "when Moses held up his hand, that Israel prevailed: and when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed." The fight in the valley follows Moses's arms on the hill. What did the raised hands mean? The text doesn't explain. It only shows. The Mishnah, a collection of Jewish teaching, asks it directly: did Moses's hands make the war or break it? Its answer: when Israel looked upward and turned their hearts to God, they prevailed. Christian readers have seen prayer in it too. And Moses gets tired. "But Moses' hands were heavy; and they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat thereon; and Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side; and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun." First a stone, so he can sit. No shame in sitting. Then one on each side, holding up an arm. They don't take the staff. They don't do his job. They just hold up what he can't hold alone anymore. Nobody tells Moses to be stronger. Heavy is allowed. Christians have read this as a picture of praying for one another and carrying each other, and some churches speak of holding up their pastors' arms. Joshua wins the battle below. But the picture that lasts is up on the hill: three people, one stone, and arms that stay up until sunset.
screen: `HANDS UP, ISRAEL PREVAILED.` · `MOSES' HANDS WERE HEAVY.` · `A STONE TO SIT ON.` · `ONE ON EACH SIDE.` · then, large: `HIS HANDS WERE STEADY UNTIL THE GOING DOWN OF THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Let your arms rest in your lap, and think of someone whose arms are heavy right now: a parent of small children, a caregiver, a nurse, a friend carrying more than their share. Picture yourself on one side of them, holding up an arm, and let one real way to help come to mind, a meal, a ride, an hour of your time. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.
Rephidim. The place where Amalek attacked Israel, and where Aaron and Hur held up Moses' arms until sunset.
Your line: hold up their arms. Nobody on that hill had to be strong alone. Day three hundred ninety-one, done.

howItsDone: Some Christians use the picture of Aaron and Hur holding up Moses's hands when they pray for their pastors, missionaries and one another, and some churches form prayer teams named for it.

chat.says: What did Aaron and Hur actually do during that battle?
options: When Moses' hands grew heavy, they sat him on a stone and held his arms up till sunset.
They led the fighters in the valley while Moses prayed alone up on the hill.
They took the staff from Moses and held it up themselves until sunset.
chat.meaning: They didn't take the staff or do his job. They gave him a stone to sit on and held up his arms, one on each side.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'the first time we meet him' and the matching myth item (superlative), 'young man' (not in Exodus 17), 'the strangest battle report in the Bible', 'many interpreters', and the k-b-d link to Pharaoh's heart (etymology; also repeated day 398's kavod-as-weight angle); the teach now cites the Mishnah (Rosh Hashanah 3:8) for the prayer reading instead of 'many Jewish and Christian interpreters'. Keeper: confirm the Mishnah paraphrase.

Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 3:8 asks whether Moses's hands made or broke the battle and answers that when Israel looked upward and subjected their hearts to God they prevailed. Paraphrased; confirm citation.
Hebrew of 17:12 kevedim (heavy) from the root k-b-d, used for Pharaoh's heart (e.g. 8:15; 9:34). Confirm.
Deuteronomy 25:18 (Amalek attacking the feeble at the rear) paraphrased as 'a later book says'.
Hur's identity is not given in Exodus; Josephus calls him Miriam's husband. Left out of the script.
Hook changed from 'tire in prayer' to 'tire on the hill': the text does not say the raised hands were prayer, and the teach presents prayer as an interpretation. Confirm.
Exodus uses k-b-d (heavy) for Pharaoh's heart in some verses and other verbs (h-z-q, q-sh-h) in others; voice softened to 'the same root ... in several places'. Confirm.
